utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in another -- in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my native language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends and colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us today our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. The main purpose of today's sitting, as you know, was to exchange -- hear your views or your submissions on the Rule 98 bis procedure that will follow immediately after the Prosecution rests its case. But of course we are also at your disposal should you have any other preliminary matters that you would like to raise or housekeeping matters that you feel are important and need to be addressed today while we have the opportunity. utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to raise the issue about the scheduling of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would expect so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And let me refer to the witness list and the numbers involved. We were able to reschedule witness number 45, Your Honour, to be -- to give testimony in court on Friday instead of the Monday. That means that this week this witness will start and the following witness will start, number 46, as that is a fixed date with a view to the agenda of that -- of that witness, on the 11th of May and we project two days for that witness. So instead of the 13th of May, we should be able to finalise we -- I mean the parties by the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop one moment, because I may have -- I want to make sure I have understood -- I have understood you. You plan to have here witness number 45 this Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will -- you will require him in the witness box until when?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On that day, Your Honour, and finalise on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the original three hours that you had indicated have now become what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Still three hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can it be three hours if we are hearing him on Friday? We usually sit for almost four hours, three hours, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So the other party can start as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am asking you how much time you require. If you require still three hours then we can plan that he will testify in-chief on Friday and that the Defence will take him on cross on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So is that fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I say "fine with you," I mean I need a confirmation that Monday will suffice for the purposes of cross-examining that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that will be plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perfect. So this is the first thing that is being decided this morning, Madam Registrar. Mr. -- does he have any protective measures, or not? None that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why I referred to numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So witness number 45 on the latest confidential amended witness list will testify this Friday, that is the 6th of May, in-chief and on Monday, the 9th of May, on cross. Right. Then I take it - this is why I intervened - that the next witness Mr. -- number 46 will start on Tuesday and not on Wednesday, as previously scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We tried to do so, Your Honour, but it is scheduled on the 11th and that's a fixed date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean a fixed date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A fixed date -- it is a date that could not be rescheduled, modified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No in other words he cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He cannot come earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When is he coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. It's on a Monday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Coming over on Monday. So the -- the problem -- Monday morning? Monday afternoon? Evening? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I learned from my co-counsel that he will be flying in Monday evening so he will be proofed on the Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can only start on the Wednesday, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Wednesday is the 11th. And do you require how many hours for that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One day, Your Honour, one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And who will be taking that witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I, too, will be requiring about one day or at the very least two and a half to three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So the second decision being taken this morning is as follows. I thank you both first of all for your cooperation and putting the Trial Chamber in a position to determine these matters beforehand so that we can manage the case in the best way possible. So witness number 46 will start his testimony on Wednesday, the 11th of May. And then on that day, the Prosecution is expected to terminate his -- to conclude his examination-in-chief. The following day, 12th, will be available for cross-examination, with the understanding that the cross-examination has to be finished, concluded, by that -- by the end of business -- by the end of the sitting on that day. And provided you am -- I take it that you still intend to bring forward witness number 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that should not create any problems for the Defence. What I would like you to do between now and this Friday when we meet again is to make a re-assessment of the would-be testimony of this witness to establish whether you require that person to testify in-chief for five hours. Because if you can finish that testimony - whoever is leading that witness, because I wouldn't know - please make a re-assessment. If you still require five hours, then it will be five hours. If we can bring that down to one day or even to, say, to four hours instead of -- or four hours roughly, then maybe on the basis of how cross-examination has been ongoing, we would require less time for cross-examination and we can finish him earlier than scheduled. Instead of taking five days or four days, we will have him for three days or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are already working on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So for the time being I think that matters of the revised witness list as far as the next -- next two weeks are concerned we -- are finally set. We -- yes, do you have any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have some additional submissions regarding several witnesses on the list to update Your Honours of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- of our plans. As we contacted the Defence regarding the three chain of custody witnesses, may I label them as such, of course meaning numbers 50, 52, and 53. There had been contacts and change of positions and we have now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but I want to make sure that in my list at least, chain of custody, I have 49, 50, and 51. Those are the numbers that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to the list, Your Honour, of the 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. I was looking at another list. Okay. So, yes, what's the position about these three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: About these three witnesses I requested co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, to address the Court. But first I want to address the Court with a view to number 49. And number 49, that is also a chain of custody witness, but solely in connection to a military log. And we considered our position in that respect, as this is a witness allowed by the Court especially with a view to the fact that this witness already testified and now it comes to the final position of the Prosecution in so far that with a view to expedite the testimonies and thus the trial, we considered to -- to propose, to request, to the Court. And it is a matter of consideration and planning to put instead of this witness our investigator, who is able to confirm via an affidavit or in person. We will request that and specify that to the Court, the fact that this military log has been handed over to him and this can be tendered as such. This military log is then -- and the handing over by that witness is the only aspect in addition to what he testified in early statement. When it comes to the credibility of the witness in -- it is already sufficiently challenged by the Defence on cross-examination, and then I mean the witness number 49, and should the Defence seek to call this witness or have any concerns about it on matters regarding his credibility, then it should be something that they would -- must raise under additional new evidence to submit to the court. And of course this new information must be relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prosecution -- Defence has no burden of proving anything in the context of what you've been saying, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This means, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the burden of proving that the testimony of this witness is a credible one; it's not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I anticipate that there are -- in the meanwhile this morning I received a letter, letter dated the 2nd of May, that addressed that issue. And I already initiate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A letter from who?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A letter from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why I anticipate in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Anyhow, we could not have a final position today, Your Honour, because the investigator concerned is, due to family circumstances, a death in the family, has left for abroad and he will return at the coming weekend. So after the coming weekend, we are able to submit a request in that respect, and I will get back to the Court and update the court for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, would you like to address the Trial Chamber on this last item that has been brought up or raised by Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I think for the most part we'll wait for the request by the Prosecution and respond to it. What Mr. Wubben has alluded to is that with the fact of the witness that is projected we had credibility issues which arose from discovery of additional evidence which we wish to put to him. So we -- all I can say now is we would be concerned if that challenge would be circumvented if that investigator would be allowed to give evidence on behalf of that witness. But as I say, until we receive the request, it's difficult to say precisely what our response would be, but I anticipate we would object to that response, meaning that the credibility issues we would wish to raise would not be open to us anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Registrar and parties and my legal officer/s [sic], I have an impression - I may be completely wrong, but I do have an impression that while that witness was giving evidence here months ago and he was being asked about the original or the copy that he had, and it was given to understand that he will be making it available and that we did make some kind of reservation, particularly for the Defence, to put questions on the -- on that document and on how -- anyway, on that document when he would be called back to round up his testimony. It's an impression that I have that we kept a window open for further questions once he had brought the original forward or made it available so that we could confront it with the copy that we had, but I may be wrong. Please do check. We will be checking, too, but I have that impression that we left that window open; in which case, in which case, the situation will change a little bit and it will change obviously in the direction of the Defence. The other thing I want to mention, and I want to make ourselves clear on this, is that as I said the burden of proving that a witness is a credible one and that the substance of his testimony is one which is trustworthy and can be relied upon and has probative value, in other words, rests with the Prosecution and not with you because we're talking of a Prosecution witness. Obviously, we do appreciate, for sure, that you may have questions that you would like to ask the witness which are -- which will address the question of credibility. Now, if this is as a -- if this is -- if this was sort of something that was reserved for already, that's one thing; if it's just an afterthought and now you want to -- you prefer to put these questions to a witness that the Prosecution for a short period of time showed interest in bringing again, I don't think we are in a position to tell or to impose on the Prosecution to bring that witness forward again. I mean, the Prosecution can always decide to drop -- to renounce having that witness come forward and testify viva voce at firsthand testimony on the military log and we certainly cannot stop the Prosecutor there. And we certainly cannot stop the Prosecutor in trying to get an investigator instead; it's their business, not ours. We will certainly not involve ourselves in that. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just in outline it's essentially similar, if not identical, situation to the one which we had before with Mr. Slavisa Eric which after the testimony testified we received material, video material which we say reflects -- will reflect on the truthfulness of the witness's answers when he testified here. And so to that extent it's not an afterthought, it's something which if we had had the material at the time we would have confronted the witness with it. So it may be that -- of course it is up to the Prosecution whom they call, but if they don't call that witness, we would be put in the situation that we had with the other witness, Mr. Eric, that we would apply for him to be recalled. So in terms of whether this is going to be a more expedient approach, it may not be if in the end we end up having to apply to have the witness brought here in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On that, if you decide to follow that direction, that procedure, you would have to apply with -- for an ad hoc motion for permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, so we reserve the possibility that we might now have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I think that now clears this matter, but please do check because I do have this recollection - I may be wrong - but I do have this recollection that since we had agreed that witness will return here with the military log and be -- plus the video that he had seen and which he had given information about, I think we had left a window open for further questions from both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll check anyway. This is being checked by us as well, so we will re-assess the situation and we will talk about this again. utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah, meaning that the other three left, and I will give the floor to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, the Prosecution recently applied to you to add a certain number of witnesses, included witness number 53. And you recently granted our motion permitting him to be added to our witness list. So what I'm about to say -- I should extend some apologies to the Trial Chamber because we are going to announce that we don't intend to call him in the interests of economy, but we did of course recently ask you to consider adding him. The reason for that is that we are interested of course in judicial economy, in trying to cut the list down as much as we can. That's witness number 53. That then leaves number 52 and number 50. I understand that - just for your information - they are military intelligence people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah, no, I just wanted to make sure. MR. DI FAZIO: So I understand also that there have been discussions in the Chamber regarding the use of the Rules to shorten their testimony. The Prosecution does not wish to adopt the provisions of Rule 92 bis in respect of either of those witnesses. It's simply too complicated to adopt all those procedures. That leaves Rule 98 (F). The evidence has got to come in some way, that's either oral or in written form. That leaves us with the current statements as they stand. We don't want to tie our hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt for a moment. I mean, dependently of Rule 92 bis. If you opt for the Rule 89 (F) procedure, they would still be required to come here to confirm the statement or not in any case. MR. DI FAZIO: Exactly, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not your wish to resort to either of the two procedures, either under 92 or under 89. Obviously we will -- we can impose, to be honest with you, following some of the decisions taken by the Appeals Chamber, we can actually impose it but we will not. I mean, it's -- especially since you're dropping one. MR. DI FAZIO: There's good reason for calling them and we -- I know you're anxious about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this stage of the proceedings, we will not interfere. MR. DI FAZIO: Furthermore, the Prosecution would be happy, if Defence agree, to try and adopt a combination of written and oral evidence which may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up to you -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- shave a few hours of the testimony. We can confer with the Defence beforehand if you wish, and see if we can mold an examination-in-chief that consists of both written and oral evidence. There's nothing in the Rules that stops that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's nothing in the Rules that stops that, but we would not intervene in imposing either of these two procedures unless we have of course an indication that you are willing -- both willing to accept, not at this stage of the proceedings. We would have provided for that at the early stages and even at pre-trial -- during the pre-trial proceedings, but not at this stage. So if there is no agreement, they will come forward and testify viva voce here. What we are interested in establishing in the shortest time possible, is the following: that you had indicated a three-hour time frame for each of these original three witnesses, which to we always seemed to be far in excess of what you would really have needed to prove or deal with the matter of chain of custody. MR. DI FAZIO: I think we can cut that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I'm asking you to do, to do the same exercise I have asked Mr. Wubben to do with regard to witness number 47 and see how much time we can cut down. I -- honestly we -- I discussed that with my legal secretary already, and of course it's something that we need to discuss amongst ourselves. But if -- we have arrived now at a stage now where we need to plan in a little bit more detail than we usually do. So in other words, if we can again save another day there, we will try to do it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I do appreciate that you have already renounced once of the witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: I think if we -- I've read the statements and they're pretty ponderous sort of statements, and if we cut to the chase, as they say, we can really probably slash 40 to 50 per cent of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, I haven't read the statements. MR. DI FAZIO: I think it's possible from the Prosecution's point of view in any event, we would finish their testimony in half a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: And then finish the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we will of course reserve our position on this until later. But if in the meantime there is a chance of having the -- again, the Prosecution and the Defence sit around the table and come to an agreement on what procedure to follow with regard to these remaining two witnesses, then of course we will accommodate you accordingly. Defence need not say anything for the time being. We'll play it by the ear. You do your homework to see how much you can cut down timewise. If you plan or you think you can cut down the testimony -- viva voce testimony in-chief to a couple of hours, both of them included, then it might not even -- might not be worth pursuing the other course of saying let's have it part in writing let's have it -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's what I meant. It's an economy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But sit down together and come back to us on this. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand what Your Honour means and we'll make sure that that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the understanding is if you come to an agreement to adopt the Rule 89, please do remember that their presence will still be required here. MR. DI FAZIO: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if -- not only -- not just for purposes of cross-examination, I mean also for the purpose of confirming. If you adopt the Rule 92 bis procedure, then the whole procedure has to be adhered to. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for clarification because we were also working for the old list that I understood the Prosecution to be dropping witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sakota.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not witness 52 on the old list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, Witness Sakota.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, in other words, the military officer witness remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't heard anything to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And two chain of custody witnesses which were 49 and 50 on the old list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did I mention the right name? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. So that deals with -- have we concluded the entire now submissions -- or the submissions on the confidential amended list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So anything else before we embark on your journey to the Rule 98 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Let me make sure that I have not forgotten anything myself. Let me go through -- no, I think we can move now to the Rule 98 bis matter. Let me introduce the subject. But before I do so, let me on behalf of the Trial Chamber thank both parties for asking for an open debate on this matter in time, before we come to the Rule 98 bis stage, in time to give an opportunity to everyone to air their views, and also to ensure that neither of the parties particularly are taken -- was taken by surprise. I believe wholeheartedly that no Trial Chamber should ever surprise the party with anything that hasn't -- they have not -- the parties with anything that they have not been given the opportunity to make submissions upon. So I thank you for allowing the Trial Chamber to discuss in an open manner, fashion, with you this problem or this issue. And I appreciate also the fact that I'm sure you've come here well-prepared to contribute in a constructive manner, thus helping the Trial Chamber come to the right decisions. You recall that Rule 98 bis was amended as a result of a decision taken by plenary. It was amended on the 8th of November. And the reason for the amendment I think emerges from the amendment itself. Reason was that our predecessors in introducing the Rule 98 bis procedure had meant to introduce a procedure within the trial that would make it possible for the trial to finish earlier if the right circumstances are obtained; but also because there was, and there still is, a very important principle pertaining to the right of the accused to remain silent involved. Basically, the whole idea behind -- the ratio behind the creation or the insertion of our rules of Rule 98 bis in its original form was the following: that the accused has a right to remain silent, and if the Prosecution has in regards -- relation to any particular count not brought forward evidence which is sufficient to sustain a conviction later on, then the accused should not be put in a position wherein he has to defend himself in any way. Unfortunately, and I say this with all responsibility, as the work of this Tribunal gathered momentum and as more cases were put on trial or came to trial, it was realised that Rule 98, instead of serving the purpose for which it was intended in the first place, was serving very little in regards of the substance of the indictment itself. Much time and much efforts were being lost in not only elaborating voluminous, lengthy motions, lengthy responses, and lengthy decisions, but also much time was being lost - I'm not saying wasted, please understand me or don't misunderstand me - in studying and evaluating single incidents and particular events on which various witnesses would have given testimony, evidence, mistaking what the substance of a Rule 98 bis motion really should be. The result was that from the moment the Prosecution rested its case to the time when the Trial Chamber would come to its decision, most of the time we would have a lapse of time of something like three months, most of the time even more than that, to be followed by the following consideration: that as we went along we realised that perhaps it would be much more practical to first hand down an oral decision disposing of the Rule 98 bis motion, to be followed then by a written decision elaborating the reasoning behind the oral decision. That is the practice, for example, that my Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case adopted, that is the practice that few other Trial Chambers adopted in other cases, too. Had we not adopted that procedure, in a complicated case like the Brdjanin case, for example, waiting for the written Rule 98 bis decision would have entailed the Trial Chamber waiting for another three weeks, maybe, or four weeks. The Judges of this Tribunal are fully aware of the time that was being dedicated to the resolution of Rule 98 bis issues, the resources of this Tribunal, which as we go along become less and not more. The fact that the longer it takes to bring a case to an end, the longer someone else will be waiting for his trial to come up, in the meantime, most of the time in a state of detention. And last but not least, the fact that we had already committed ourselves to an exit -- completion strategy made us think twice about the following: whether to retain Rule 98 bis, as it was, until the 8th of December; whether to abolish it outright; and lastly, whether to amend it with a view to on one hand respect and secure the due-process rights of the accused, which -- to which I referred to earlier, namely right to remain silent -- right to remain silent, vis-a-vis put in juxtaposition to what the Prosecution would have been able to bring by way of evidence. So that's on the one side. On the other side, the interests and the responsibility of this Tribunal to ensure that this legal instrument of procedure that we had created way back in the late 1990s no longer served to length -- to prolong the duration of the case, but if anything served to -- its practical purpose for which it was meant and created in the first place. So we opted for this last -- third alternative. And as you noticed, there are some differences between the previous Rule 98 bis and the current Rule 98 bis provision. For the benefit of anyone who is following these proceedings and is not familiar with the legal and technical problems involved, I will very briefly say the following. I will read first and foremost what Rule 98 bis provided before it was amended in December. In its paragraph A, that Rule provided that: "An accused may file a motion for the entry of judgement of acquittal on one or more offences charged in the indictment within seven days after the close of the Prosecution's case and in any event prior to the presentation of evidence by the Defence pursuant to Rule 85(A)(ii)." You will immediately notice, having heard me read out this first paragraph from the previous Rule 98 bis -- now, this was essentially party-driven. The whole process of the Rule 98 bis procedure was part -- triggered by the party. It would be the accused who had the right to ask the Trial Chamber to consider a motion for acquittal. You will also agree with me, for sure, that this seven-day time limit was many a time extended not to another seven days but sometimes to weeks, months. I recall instances where it was extended to even a month and a half, almost two months. And in some complicated cases, given what -- what it entailed, particularly the fact that it had to be a written one, I am not -- I am not that much surprised. The second paragraph of the previous Rule 98 bis provided that: "The Trial Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal on motion of an accused or proprio motu if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." So from the party-driven stage, we now move to the discretion or the -- the role of the Trial Chamber to dispose of the matter. And you will notice also that already there was the possibility -- the window open for the Trial Chamber to dispose of questions of acquittal after the end of the Prosecution case also proprio motu, in other words short of an ad hoc motion by the Defence there was still the right - I'm not saying that there was the responsibility. Please do not read me out -- in that direction - there may have been, but there was the possibility for the Trial Chamber to decide that there was -- I will use a phrase that I use in my own county, no case to answer in relation to one or more counts. If that was the case, it would have entailed giving the opportunity to the parties to be heard on that, obviously, because as I said in the earlier on -- Trial Chamber would never have thought of giving a surprise to the Prosecution in any case. So that would have been open for debate and the Prosecution would have consulted. But the -- in other words, if in the case the Defence had opted not to trigger the Rule 98 bis motion, there was always the right of the Trial Chamber to dispose of same issues proprio motu. Problems, as you are well aware, arose as to what was the standard to be used when the Trial Chamber came to its decision, either on a motion of acquittal or on -- or on proprio motu initiative. Undoubtedly there have been some different opinions expressed in decisions forthcoming from different Chambers, especially in the early parts when this -- earlier stages when this -- the then-existing Rule 98 bis was being applied. I will not dwell on the reasons for that. The position seems to me to have been resolved by the Appeals Chamber, particularly in the Blaskic case - but not only in the Blaskic case, there were several other decisions that followed suit - that spelled out in no unclear terms the standard that ought to be adopted in the Rule 98 bis exercise, and it is the standard that is adopted in all the common-law systems, jurisdictions that I am -- I am familiar with. And this, again, I don't think we need to go into. The standard has been set and it is not going to change. And I will be explaining to you that the change in the wording in the new Rule 98 bis does not mean that the standard has been changed; it only means that the road which should be taken should involve the parties and the Trial Chamber in much less work than it used to into December. And I will explain to this later on. The Rule was changed, as you know, in December, and both existing -- it was a new rule that has come into place. And basically what it says now in its first paragraph is that the close -- "at the close" -- in its paragraph, "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." You will notice that the whole procedure is no longer really party-driven. And you will also notice that the new Rule 98 bis motion does not say that at the close of the Prosecutor's case the Trial Chamber "may," but it says "shall." So the first message, or the first conclusion to be drawn on the face of it from this new Rule 98 bis -- Rule 98 bis is that it has become mandatory now for the Trial Chamber to embark on this Rule 98 bis acquittal exercise at the end of the Prosecutor's case and need not wait for the Defence to file or to make any application for the acquittal of the client. So that is point number one, and I would like you to understand it from the very beginning. Next thing, it says "by oral decision." So you will immediately notice that what previously was essentially a written decision has now become an oral decision. Let me explain something which -- the only thing that I think is relevant in this context. The fact that we are now saying by oral decision does not in any way diminish or do away with the duty of the Trial Chamber to make sure that its oral decision is a reasoned one. Prior to the amendment in December 1998 there would have been a written decision, even in most cases it was preceded by an oral decision. In both the oral decision and -- but particularly in the written decision, the decision to acquit or not to acquit was always motivated and the reason is not only because giving reasoned decision is a matter of natural justice, it's a modern development in the area or in the concept of natural -- principles of natural justice, for those who believe in natural justice; for those who do not believe in natural justice, it still remains a principle of justice. I'm saying that because I know that in some areas it's almost an anathema to mention the word "natural justice." So -- but I'm used to it and I mention it. So that's number one. And secondly because there has never been any doubt at all that, although very rarely resorted to, there's still a right of appeal from decisions taken on the Rule 98 bis -- on a Rule 98 bis motion. And I said there have been very few instances, but there have been. What Trial Chambers have done is that most of the time they have ensured - and that includes also the trial - the Appeals Chamber, they have ensured first that the appeals were dealt with and determined with the utmost celerity; and secondly, the case, the trial will not stop pending the determination of the appeal. For these same reasons, I need hardly, therefore, repeat to you that our oral decision will of course be a reasoned one, be a reasoned one. So do not expect any surprises on the -- in that context. And of course -- and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, basically this means that you will both be given the opportunity to be heard, to make submissions, if you want to make submissions. No one will be forced to make submissions. And after that, we are then expected by the new Rule 98 bis to enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. Previously, you would have noticed that the wording was -- "if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." And now you have the use of the word "count" and not "offences charged," as you had previously in Rule 98 bis. You have a specific reference to the count itself, which in common-law tradition is the matter that is a matter that counts, it's the count itself. And instead of saying "the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." We are saying if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction, and what you don't many read is "under that count." So is there a difference between "if the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction" or "if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction"? It is my submission to you, that there is absolutely no difference at all in the approach. The only difference in what there is -- is what I'm going to try to explain. We tried, in formulating the simple, straightforward words of the new Rule 98 bis, we tried to do our best to level out once and for all the different sort of kinds of approach and methodology that was being adopted in the course of the Rule 98 bis motion, mostly due to the different jurisdictions from which each one of us comes and mostly due to not having, probably for some of us, worked or experienced with Rule 98 bis procedure. We tried to level out the various differences and also to level out the various approaches to bring them in line with what had, by December, the end of last year, become the standard pronunciation of the standard that was applicable on rule after rule of repeated decisions by the Appeals Chamber. Basically, if in relation to a particular count the Prosecution has brought forward evidence that in terms of the previous Rule 98 bis would be described as being insufficient to sustain a conviction, forget the words on that or those charges because those -- this is where the problems arose most of the time. If the Prosecution did not -- provided evidence which was insufficient to sustain a conviction, basically the conclusion that the Trial Chamber would come to is that there is no evidence that has been brought forward by the Prosecution that is capable of supporting a conviction under that count. So you have noticed that in the same sentence I have used the previous expression and the new expression. "Bringing forward evidence which is insufficient to sustain a conviction" is tantamount to not having brought evidence capable of supporting a conviction. So don't expect the Trial Chamber to give to the two versions, the old and the new, a different interpretation. I hope I have made myself clear on this. I'm trying to use as simple a language as possible so as to avoid confusion, knowing also that in whichever direction I look I know that there are mixed jurisdictions and mixed legal experiences and practices. We have changed also the wording, the phraseology. We no longer say what we had in paragraph (A) in the previous version. We don't talk of acquittal on one or more offences charged in the indictment, which could have been understood to mean that each -- that each count was to be divided into various offences or that the events charged in a particular counts could be equiparated with offences rather than events and are underlying facts. And we have tried also to avoid what was contained in the second paragraph of that previous Rule 98 bis, the last words "on that or on those charges." Because in reality, if you look across the Rules we see that, as often happens in most common-law jurisdictions, the word "charge" and "count" are used interchangeably. In my county, for example, technically speaking a person is charged until he comes to trial; he comes to trial as an accused. So at that point in time, he is no longer charged, he is accused. We make that distinction. But in most common-law jurisdictions, basically when you speak of a count, you are speaking of a charge; when you speak of a charge, for the purposes of trial proceedings, you are speaking of a count. In order to try and streamline as much as possible the phraseology used throughout the Rules, we have opted for "count" rather than "offences charged" or "charges," with the understanding that everyone will try to understand that behind the purpose of Rule 98 bis, there is not - and please, I repeat it again, there is not a humungous exercise to be undertaking to deal with the minutiae of the events mentioned during the testimony and trying to establish whether a particular event has been proven or not proven or whether we should concentrate on issues of credibility or issues of authenticity, et cetera. Please, I'm making it very clear: There will be no submissions made or received on issues of authenticity and credibility at this stage; those will be reserved until later, if the case proceeds. There will equally not be much entertainment of submissions, which rather than concentrating on whether the evidence is submitted -- brought forward is sufficient to sustain a conviction under a particular count would deal with the minutiae of certain particular events. The direction that we would like to lead you to is the following: We have a case, a trial, with an articulated indictment, consisting of six counts, six precise counts. What we will decide ultimately, after hearing your submissions, is, for example, if under Count 1 the Prosecution had adduced evidence capable of sustaining a conviction under that count or not, and simply that. We will of course be prepared to hear evidence if there is a submission that, for example, in regard to a particular person mentioned in the indictment that's supposed to have been the victim of cruel treatment or the victim of murder, it's the submission of the Defence that there was absolutely no evidence at all adduced by the Prosecution or that the evidence adduced is -- can never sustain a conviction. Then I think - and we have discussed this amongst ourselves - we will entertain submissions, short submissions, on that score because ultimately it will be in the benefit of the economy of justice that the Defence is put on notice that as far as regards the alleged murder of, for example, Rado Pejic -- let me not mention names, as regards the alleged murder of -- there's absolutely no way that the Trial Chamber can ultimately come to a conviction so that they don't have to lose or waste time in trying to bring forward evidence in that regard, even though they have no burden of proof, but particularly because they have a right to remain silent. So that right ought to be -- ought to be respected. Submissions relating to details, I think we can -- you can spare us those. We don't need detailed submissions. Please concentrate on where you believe that the Prosecution has not proved -- brought evidence within the standard mentioned and set forth by the Appeals Chamber. We would expect the Prosecution to stand up and say, We believe that we do not have a leg to stand upon. We believe that we have not adduced sufficient evidence according to the standard, to sustain a conviction under Count 1, Count 2, Count 3, or Count 4, if you believe so. I know that has been done in the past. I know that I am dealing with an office that is highly responsible and has not hesitated in pointing out to the Trial Chamber these shortcomings or weaknesses in the Prosecution's case. After all, I believe that apart from the role that the Prosecution has of prosecuting, you have also got the role of being and ensuring to be the best friend of the accused in such like proceedings in the high tradition of trial procedure that we are all used to. So we would expect you to address the Trial Chamber immediately, even before we give the floor to the Defence, when we come to that stage, should you believe there are such weaknesses in your case. We do not wish to hear any submissions by you, in particular trying to explain why you believe that you have proved your case within the Rule 98 bis standard in each and every area. If an area is contested to you by the Defence, then do so by all means, you will respond and try to contest and make submissions, your own submissions, on that. If there is one count, for example, in particular which -- or parts of a count that the Defence does not really make submissions upon, if it goes through that exercise, which it might not do after all, then please don't waste our time; we will do that exercise at the end of the day because we are tasked with a responsibility. But otherwise, we don't need to hear unnecessary -- unnecessary submissions on what is not being contested. Then there is one final matter before I come to -- there are, for example, as in Counts 5 and 6, instances where the accused is being charged under 7(1) as a mode of responsibility, and there are instances where he is being charged under 7(3) as a mode of responsibility. Submissions on the alleged modes -- mode of responsibility will of course be received because they relate to the various counts that we have and are the basis of the various counts. So I need not dwell on this matter any further. I think it should be self explanatory. When we say as in Rule 98 bis as amended, we will hear oral submissions of the parties obviously on the counts of whether there is sufficient evidence to sustain a conviction on any count. It means also evidence -- sorry, submission on the alleged -- not only on the events having happened, not only on the mens rea and the actus reus of the accused, but also on the mode of responsibility attributed to him in terms of the indictment. So I think I have made that clear and I don't think I need to explain. Last point before we have a break, and that will give you half an hour time to -- then to say your own is then question of what's going to happen as soon as -- towards the end of May or early June, at the latest, the Prosecution rests its case. Let me say straightaway that I know that although at the domestic level, as I have tried to explain on various occasions, this is a procedure that is -- immediately Mr. Wubben stands up and says -- we hear "the Prosecution rests its case," most of the time there is not even a break. You look the other side and say, Any submissions this direction? I would listen to what you have to say and many instances dealing with cases that involve a very short number of days -- a few days, and a very short number of witnesses, there would be absolutely no difficulty at all for the Magistrate or Judge to take a decision which be oral infallibly. But here, I understand the cases are more complicated. I, for one, referring to that particular witness which you are seeking to bring again or which the Defence might wish to recall, I don't recall vividly each and every moment of his testimony, but I -- although I do recall a lot. So I do understand and we -- when I say "I," I say we have discussed this at length over the past days and we do understand that these cases before this Tribunal are somewhat different. But you also need to understand that the procedure that we will ultimately adopt will not render for all intents and purposes useless or futile the whole purpose of the amended Rule 98 bis. In other words, the whole exercise is to make sure that we address ourselves to what traditionally were applicable Rule 98 bis processes for acquittal after the Prosecution case should be -- should seek to achieve and should ultimately mean. That's number one. Not -- in other words, not to involve ourselves in examining certain details that need not be examined. And secondly, to ensure that the whole exercise is speedily concluded, speedily concluded. We will have a break now. And as soon as we return in half an hour's time, of course I will -- you will all, both, have an opportunity to return to make submissions on what I have said. And in particular, also with regard to this last part of my intervention, particularly what are your intentions, evil or benign, as there might -- as they might be, then ultimately we will decide and we will let you know beforehand what our decision will be. We are open, of course, to any constructive suggestions that you may have. We will be fully aware of your needs, but you also need to keep in mind making any submissions that we have responsibility to shoulder. Unfortunately, it has fell on this Trial Chamber to deal with this matter first because in the Limaj case, apparently, the parties have renounced to resorting to the procedure. They have -- they will not be making any submissions. So the role of the Trial Chamber has become much easier there. We'll here what you have to say. Then you will have our decision later on, which would give you roughly a good month in advance -- advanced notice and knowledge of what to expect. And then we will act accordingly. I thank you for listening, and we will resume in 30 minutes' time, that is 5 minutes past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can proceed. If there is any point on what I have stated that you think I need to expand or explain further, please let me know. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my submission will be short in time. The Prosecution is much obliged with the clarifications done in the submissions by Your Honours prior to the break. It clarifies the Trial Chamber's opinion in such a way that it will be supportive to parties to know in advance what direction the approach should take with a view to the procedure, as well as to the standard applied, too. We shared this outcome of the opinions submitted by the Trial Chamber. Again, it will be a support for us because it's also clarified further by the Presiding Judge, and that means that we also adopt the standards and the set of the submission as projected by this Trial Chamber. That's why I can be short in time with my submission, only in addition two points, but that's additional. The first issue is, then, that the Prosecution would like -- that's in the phase prior to the 98 bis submission would like to revisit the issue of the agreed facts among parties, meaning, for example, an armed -- international armed conflict as such as a potential agreed fact. This is an example, but we would like to revisit that and to contact the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hadn't you withdrawn that from the indictment itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, the international part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, the international part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But the armed conflict as such. I mean an example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Anyhow, we would like to prefer to contact the Defence in order to propose to them and to learn their position in that respect, also to expedite the trial in such a way that even in advance it is clear that we can trim our case as regarding the facts. That's one issue. The second issue is the scheduling as such after, so subsequent, to the finalisation of the Prosecution case. There is then, first as we perceive it, the submission by Defence counsel; then subsequent, submission by the Prosecution. We should be able to address the submission by Defence counsel fully and to do it in a professional way, and we will do so, meaning also that we are interested in time scheduled for a break between those two submissions and we would like to learn the opinion of the Trial Chamber in that regard because what might be supportive if that break is short in time that the Defence is able to give prior notice to the parties, including the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, of the issues that will be addressed in their submission. So if the break is short in time, that will certainly expedite the proceeding as such. We should be able, then, given the fact that there is a prior notice, let's say one or two weeks in advance, that we are able to already work on the preparing of those issues. And we would like to learn the opinion of the Trial Chamber, and that is also an aspect I believe the Trial Chamber will be supportive upon that decision-making whenever the Trial Chamber by itself learn to what length the submission is intended by the Defence. And this also gets back to the general observation that, and I quote you, Your Honour, "neither party should be taken by surprise," as such. Including, that's my conclusion, that there's time to prepare. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Who is going to deal with this? Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I will, and I might just put the lectern up, if you just give me a moment. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to firstly just say some general -- well, give some general comments about Rule 98 bis and then come to the points made by my learned friend in response. And firstly, I just wanted to say a little about the virtue, if you like, and the importance of Rule 98 bis from the Defence side. Firstly, everything Your Honour said this morning confirms our understanding of the new Rule 98 bis, namely, obviously, that it's oral but that it's -- no longer party-driven, to a certain extent a proprio motu power of the Chamber, that there would be a reasoned decision and possible right of appeal. Arguably that would involve leave, but that's a peripheral matter. In terms of the virtue and importance of Rule 98 bis, I wanted to emphasise that a little bit, partly because Your Honour suggested last week that it might be something which in a practical spirit we could bypass and go straight on to the Defence case. I just wanted to say that for our part, if we will make a Rule 98 bis submission - which we will do, I can confirm that now - it's because we genuinely believe it should succeed. If we make it for the whole of the Prosecution case that it should succeed entirely, and that we should all be prepared to go home; in our case, literally go home, figuratively for the other parties. The case will be over in June. If we make a submission, we're not just going through the motions of making a motion which we know will not proceed, we think that the Prosecution has not made out the essential elements of their case. So going back to the general elements of Rule 98 bis. I think it would be impossible to abolish it altogether because of course if the Prosecution has to prove X, Y, and Z, and those are essential elements what they have to prove, if they haven't proved X, let's say, then obviously there's no point of going on to the Defence case, there's no point as a practical matter, because that's months of trial, tens of witnesses, hundreds of thousands or Euros or dollar which have been spent when it needed by because the Prosecution hadn't established the basics of what they need to establish. And there is also, as Your Honour said, a point of principle which is if the Prosecution hasn't even made out the outlines of their case, then the defendant is not called upon to bring witnesses to answer a case which hasn't even been made out. Your Honour referred to the right to remain silent. Just for purposes of clarification, I understand that to mean the right not to call witnesses on his behalf, because of course the right of the accused to remain silent remains throughout the Defence case. And indeed I would even go so far as to say that given the difference in threshold between a prima facie case and beyond a reasonable doubt, it could even be that you have an unsuccessful submission, no evidence called by the Defence and still an acquittal. In any event, that's all just by way of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, I agree entirely with you, Mr. Jones. It has never been doubted indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour referred to the history of this Rule. I think what's important in the light of what I was just saying about the virtue and importance of Rule 98 bis, it may be that in the past it has been somewhat abused, in the sense that perhaps sometimes there was applications that have been made which should not have been made because there was clearly a prime facie case and written submissions had become lengthier and lengthier. So that eventually one had two trials, two sets of lengthy pleadings, at the close of the Prosecution case and then again at the close of trial. That's why we're adamantly in agreement with the Chamber that this should be absolutely an oral proceeding and it shouldn't slip back into a proceeding in which there are exchange of written pleadings. And that will bring me in a moment to Mr. Wubben's request for written filings in advance of the application. As far as the test is concerned, I think that that too is clear and it was helpful, for Your Honours' confirmation, that the test is the same. And in fact -- I suppose in other words it's because evidence must be sufficient to sustain a conviction for the case to go ahead. So in other words, if there's not sufficient evidence, then it stops there. It makes perfect sense. There's the test which we're familiar with in the common-law jurisdictions of whether a reasonable trier of fact could convict on the evidence, but I think it's much of a muchness that these are the same sort of tests. So again it's to -- we can confirm from our part that our submissions will be very focussed as to there being no evidence or practically no evidence on certain elements and we won't make extensive submissions about the weight which should be accorded different items of evidence and certainly not to all sorts of matters which are not directly pertinent. And again just for a general understanding, my understanding from my experience in the UK is that a submission would be, for example, where you have a crime like facilitating a legal entry or gain - and we would submit gain has not been shown, no evidence whatsoever of gain - and if we're right it's over; or murder, where there is no proof of death --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I think it is worth interrupting you. This is precisely the way we look at it. And you can imagine, each and every count here has got its legal ingredients requirement. And if you think that the Prosecution case should stop because one of these requirements has not been fulfilled, that's what you should concentrate on and we don't want to hear submissions on the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. And it may be, and to anticipate a point I was going to deal with later, when we deal with command responsibility, there are clear cumulative elements which have to be shown by the Prosecution and there is no dispute as to what those elements are. And it may be that our submission might be just on, let's say, the very first one or the second one, and simply that that element has not been shown, and of course it follows that if that element has not been shown then the whole thing falls through because they are cumulative elements. If we do take that approach, and we don't wish it to be understood that we are conceding that there is a sufficient case on any of the other points, it's simply that we wish to make a focussed submission on our stronger points and that's the approach we will be adopting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few clarifications on our part. As Your Honour said this is no longer party-driven and looking at the rule it's no longer evident that it's clearly a motion by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not. It is clear that it is not a motion by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, which does raise questions to the procedure in which order the parties will make their submissions. It may be the practical approach the Prosecution first indicate they are conceding any counts; that we would then make a more substantive submission. The Prosecution would respond and then we would reply. That's what we would propose would be a good procedure and we can discuss in a moment whether breaks would be appropriate or not. As far as the oral procedure is concerned, we would understand that this wouldn't preclude us for using, for example, skeleton arguments or any sort of material which will just aid presentation, which would be passed out on the day just simply to help Your Honours follow our submissions. But if that's something which the Chamber decides it would vitiate the oral nature of the procedure, then we're of course prepared not to do that. It would be only to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll deal with this. I thank you for raising this matter because it had been in my mind and I forgot to mention it myself. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We would also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will come to it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would also envision and welcome an interactive procedure as well, in which -- since after all it's Your Honours who we would be seeking to persuade, we would see it that Your Honours would feel free interrupt at different points and put questions. In that way it could be -- it would be more expedited, certainly, but it would make more sense if we're effectively able to persuade Your Honours, if any doubts Your Honours have are able to put to us during the hearing. Yes. As far as two points made by my learned friend, two requests perhaps. Firstly, agreed facts. It's something which -- we're always open to discussions with the Prosecution on any subject, but I think as far as agreed facts are concerned we would say it's a bit late in the day for that. Because if the Prosecution is asking us to agree a fact it's because it wasn't proved during their case and their case will be over shortly. When we're talking about 98 bis, their case will be over and if they haven't proved a fact which they think they should have proved at that point, I hardly see that we're going to agree that fact. As far as the schedule is concerned, we are really in favour of a very expedited oral procedure, really to the point of where we would be happy with the last witness being heard on Friday, I think it's the -- I'm not sure of the exact date, the 27th or the 28th, and we would make a submission on the following Monday. And we thought even a week without breaks, two days for the Defence to make their submissions, two days for the Prosecution to respond, and a day for us to reply, would mean we could have the whole procedure dealt with in a week, which firstly would set a very good precedent for first application of this Rule, to show that it can be dealt with in an expeditious way. And secondly, because any breaks -- well, particularly breaks in which it is proposed written notice be given would delay the procedure by weeks, really, and I'll say why. If the Prosecution said, Well, we have to have notice of the points we're going to make and they want a week for something for that to happen, we of course have an equal right to receive notice or to have a break anyway to reply on their response and the whole thing would get drawn out into June, when frankly I think it's in all our interests to have this proceeding dealt with in the first half of June. But as a matter more of principle rather than planning. Firstly as the Prosecution closes their case, we can't notify them of the points we are going to take because that would be tantamount to alerting them to things they haven't proved. So if we were to say before they close their case, Oh, actually you haven't produced any evidence on this point, then they can come back and fill that gap and we would have done the Prosecution a favour, which it's not any part of our duty to do. So one can only contemplate the starting point of any notice coming once the Prosecution case closes. So as I say you have delays already from the procedure we are proposing where we start straight in on Monday after the last witness is heard on Friday. And if we, the Defence, who after all are going to be doing most of the running on this motion, if we are prepared to go straight in after the trial closes, then we say the Prosecution should be willing to do the same. But perhaps more fundamentally as a point of principle, this isn't a motion where the Prosecution is going to be surprised or ambushed by anything, because quite simply we are going to be making submissions that insufficient evidence is produced on certain counts. The Prosecution absolutely should know at this stage what they say proves each element and each count. The Prosecution should know right now that let's say for Bjelovac proof that subordinates of our client committed the crimes, they should be able to say this witness and the other witness. It's something which they should have to hand immediately. And so it should be something they should respond to immediately when we say there has not been sufficient evidence. There is nothing coming from left field, as they say, which will surprise the Prosecution. If we were to make legal arguments which would involve arguing on the basis of authority, and I can see the Prosecution saying can we be alerted beforehand if you're going to be relying on this authority or that authority or make this legal argument. That's fair enough. But these are factual matters which -- we've all been following the evidence given in this case and there's no reason at all why the Prosecution shouldn't be able to immediately respond on our submissions. Just two -- some final points as well to clarify our understanding. We agree entirely that authenticity and credibility are not issues which we would be getting into, which is partly a reflection of the fact that you would be taking the Prosecution's evidence at its highest, to a certain extent. However, of course, if there is a document which Prosecution was relying on and it has been shown to a witness and the witness says that doesn't reflect the reality, or it hasn't been shown to any witness, then of course we will reserve the right to say that document has no probative value because it hasn't been confirmed by any witness. That's not really an authenticity issue, it's just to say we may make submissions on documents. Also, in terms of the way we would structure our submissions, we would, as Your Honour suggested and as we've confirmed, address very specific elements and counts in a very focussed way; however, to do that it may be that there is a chain of reasoning which -- which has to be followed where we would first have to say on in general subject there has been no evidence of such, and then another area, and then that would lead to the conclusion that there was insufficient evidence on that count. So to alert Your Honours that we may deal in other matters, but in a directly relevant way which I will be happy during the course of submissions to explain the relevance. And we also may structure our submissions not necessarily in the order of the counts. We might do them in another order. But I'm sure that's all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for that particular purpose, may I put it to you, Mr. Jones, that I believe you should be the one -- in other words, when I say "you," it's the Defence that should be the one to go first and not the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, because otherwise the Prosecution would feel to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope that's agreeable to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I have always seen it and I want to make sure that you fully agree with this approach: Defence should go first, choose the way to present their case for acquittal, and then you will respond, preferably trying to keep to the same pattern or the same order of arguments as presented by the Defence, if that -- but of course you will have other options available if you want to. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and unless I can assist Your Honours further, that's really all I wanted to say. And really just to reiterate that we're in favour of the most expedited oral proceeding conceivable. We think it's a good precedent to set and that we are opposed to any filing of notice and what not, because -- it's particularly also for this reason: That if we were to give notice or have to be obliged to give notice to the Prosecution of their points and possibly the converse from their side, we would be in a situation where, as with any written submissions, if we omitted something it would be open to the Prosecution to still claim, oh, well, we've been ambushed, we didn't know this point was going to be taken. It would be open to the Prosecution to say this is obviously a point the Defence has just thought up because they didn't put it in their notice. And generally, as with any written submission, it puts pressure on us to have a full, written submission to make sure that we're fully entitled to raise the points in the oral hearing. So I would submit that very quickly we would slide back into a written procedure and that the only way really to ensure that the spirit of the rule is observed is for it to be fully oral, albeit with aids on the day, skeletons, and what not, which might assist Your Honours to understand and follow the submissions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. I'll try to address all the points raised, with the understanding that some of these points obviously we have not had time to discuss amongst ourselves. So Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, as I go along if there is anything that you want to reserve your position upon or disagree with me, just stop me. We will have a short break and we will discuss outside, just in case I say anything with which you're not in agreement. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Wubben, do you want to respond to what has been mentioned by Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In short, and focussed on the prior notice, that that's an issue that's driven -- not to be informed in detail but is driven by the argument that we should give a specific response to a submission -- an oral submission by Defence counsel regarding 98 bis. That means that this Defence counsel that select the details for that submission and if we are then able to respond directly to that, that will be a -- quite an effort to comply with all the issues that will be -- will be dealt with by the Defence. Rather, if the Defence is afraid of giving away their position or giving away the possibility that -- or not giving away, but put the Prosecution in the position that we know that our evidence might be weak or not, that that can be avoided by giving us as much as possible the issues and not putting it in a way like, these are the issues we will address, but the caveat in this moment in time, we will inform you of these issues we will address during that submission. And anyhow, in preparing it it's easy to say that we have the factual information available. Yes, we have; but to put it in a manner that will address efficiently and effective the submission of the Defence, that is step two and apart from that there are also, apart from the factual allegations, there are also the legal elements and the legal questions, preliminary questions, to dispute and then to deal with. The second part, that last part, briefly also to the skeleton issue raised by the Defence counsel. As I envisaged when I looked at the Trial Chamber decision in the Brdjanin case and in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case regarding 98 bis, there is this framework of first the preliminary questions and then focussed on general legal elements. And then it comes to the factual parts of the counts, and then subsequent to the legal parts of the count. Now, this -- this can be followed as such, meaning -- meaning that framework is a kind of proof of technology and enable parties to give a kind of overall skeleton for their submission. I'm much obliged that Defence counsel raised this because it will also serve and support the Prosecution. When it comes -- and that's my latest point -- filling in the date of the -- of the 98 bis submission, to starting of it, and now already speaking about the mandate to start subsequent to the end of May, for me, that is really speculation. I don't know to what extent the submission will be by the Defence. I don't know the specific date, the last date. We are still in the phase of rescheduling our witnesses. Depending on these circumstances, I would prefer and advise Trial Chamber to learn first more information and then not to jump right away, but give both parties the time to prepare for their submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's have a very short break. I -- everyone needs -- will stay here, wait a little bit, because we'll only be a couple of minutes out just to make sure that we are fine-tuned, as we usually are on practically everything. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the accused is here as well. So I thank you both, Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben. We've had a short discussion in the meantime. The idea is to ensure that we are fine-tuned, the three Judges, as possible. As I said, we are almost always very well fine-tuned. Let me try and take a few points that have been raised one by one, but before I do so let me make also one thing clear which I failed to mention earlier on and this relates to the retroactive application of the amended Rule. You know as much as we do, that we have Rule 6(D) of our Rules which provides that "An amendment shall enter into force after seven days of issue of an official Tribunal document containing an amendment, but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or of a convicted or acquitted person in any pending case." I have not heard any submissions, and I would have expected those submissions to come from my right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have not heard any submissions that -- to the effect that the application of the current Rule 98 bis would prejudice the rights of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and for the record I should just confirm that we don't wish -- we wouldn't say that it prejudices the accused's rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I thank you, Mr. Jones, for clearing that. Now, let's start with the other matters raised. Agrees facts. Of course, Mr. Wubben, I do and we all appreciate your effort to have this exercise carried out before you come to the stage of making final submissions on the Rule 98 bis exercise. I do see the importance of it. But short of the Defence adhering -- agreeing with you, adhering to your request, we can do nothing about it. I mean, this question of agreed facts at this stage of the proceedings is, in my view, nothing that the Trial Chamber should involve itself with. It involved itself with it during the pre-trial stage, as you recall. We made an effort to see if you could come halfway. After that, you had both filed written submissions on this matter and agree on a few facts and disagreed on the crucial. I think, Mr. Wubben, if Mr. Jones doesn't want to cooperate with you on this, which is his prerogative, it is his choice, I would suggest to you that you do not try to involve us in the exercise. The question of -- I come to the next point. The question of how much information and in what form should it be -- should it be exchanged between the parties.
