My clear message to you is the following: You are of course free to exchange between yourselves notes and information as to what points you are going to cover during the submissions and any further information that you might like or be ready to disclose to the other side, but please don't try to use this as a means of reverting to the old system of written submissions. You are also free, because this point was raised by Mr. Jones, during your submissions to present -- make presentations -- I don't know what you might have in mind. But if you think that your submissions may be enhanced and be projected better by means of, I don't know, a chart for example, a chart explaining, for example, what, according to you, was the chain of command, well you're free to do that. But if what you meant was essentially reducing into writing the submissions that you would make orally, then that will be resisted because that would be tantamount to reverting in a clandestine manner to the old regime of having written submissions when the idea is to do away with those written submissions. In other words -- because I am trying to read into your minds. If this is intended as notes which would be a sort of a -- an aid to the Trial Chamber to try and focus better on the points made during the oral submissions, I thank you very much, we don't need it because we will have the transcript in any case and we will be able to look at the transcript whenever we need to look at the transcript. If it's other matters that you think will help you advance better the points that you are trying to make during the oral submissions, yes, of course, depending on what they will be, you will have every chance of doing that. But please use your discretion. The standard rule should be, we have changed, switched, from a written procedure to a distinctly oral one and it -- we should honour our commitment and make sure that it remains an oral one. That's all. Okay. Can I ask Mr. Jones on behalf of the Trial Chamber to, yes, tell you beforehand what his submissions are going to be or at least some kind of submissions. And first of all, I see a lot of value in the point made by him that until the very last word coming from the mouth of your very last witness has been uttered, I don't think he should even be in a position to speak up. After all, as you all know, he is not bound to stand up and tell you what he is going to submit two days later or three days later. I mean, it's -- so we will not raise that matter with Mr. Jones, with Mr. Jones. It's a matter of maybe further contact between you as we approach the D-Day, as we approach the debate on Rule 98 bis. I am confident that the relations that have existed so far to date between the two sides, barring certain minor incidents which, you know, they are normal tiffs which happen one minute and are forgotten the next, I think the relationship has been very positive and I have no reason to doubt that it will remain to be so. I mean, judging from what Mr. Jones himself has said, if, for example, when he stands up to start with his submissions, he intends to make submissions as to whether a particular crime, for example, particular crime existed at the time when it's supposed to have been committed under international customary law, for example, and he wants to make submissions on that, he should put you on notice of. Because obviously if he doesn't and that happens, it will have caught both you and us unawares. We are in a position to allow ourselves as much time as we need and we don't have to respond, while you have to respond. And that would be tantamount to putting you in a position which you can then ask for time to study the matter and then come forward to address. So it's a question I think you should use your good sense, both of you, and continue in the fruitful interaction that there has been and cooperation there has been between you until the very end. Mr. Jones also mentioned that he would prefer to have some kind of interaction with the Trial Chamber as this process develops. Yes, by all means. And I can also tell you that we will need our time as well to decide because we have a greater responsibility, actually, thrust on our shoulders than one would imagine. So we'll go through everything, and it's not to be excluded that we may encounter some problems which you may have not -- which you may have missed completely, in which case it is not to be excluded that we can also, we may also come back to you in open sitting, obviously, and ask you to address the matter. Let me make myself clear on this because I don't want to mislead you. Let's take for an instance, certain example, neutral example, Mr. Jones stands up and he says on Count 2, for example, cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war. His submission would be, for example, as regards this count, these are the formal legal requirements and these are the ingredients or the elements of the actus reus. We submit that Prosecution has not adduced sufficient evidence to sustain an indictment, in so far as this and this and that is concerned. Full stop. Finished. And let's suppose that you will be very laconic in your response and your submission would be, We beg to disagree, we beg to disagree. Our submission is that this has been amply proved within the parameters of the standards set. So let's say that is the position. And then let's say when we are doing our homework with -- amongst ourselves, also with the help of our staff, we find out that there is some, for example, damning evidence that would not -- and that would never really explain how on earth Mr. Jones even thought for a moment that you had not proven that case. We are not going to come back to you at that point. We are not going to tell you, Mr. Jones, please look to the evidence of Mr. XY, transcript page, et cetera, lines -- so 1 to 20. That you should have looked at before you stood up and took the plunge. In other words, when I say that we may come back to you on certain issues, it means to have a clarification, not to fill in where you have left out. In other words, we come to you where we think we need some clarification which would help us to come to a conclusion. I'm not saying that we definitely will come back, but I'm not excluding that we might come back. That's the point I wanted to make. During the discussion itself, during the submissions itself, we would have already of course started, like you have already, started doing our homework on the Rule 98 bis. In other words, don't expect a situation to obtain on the first day when you start with your submissions that we will have in the courtroom where we will be working that day, the Defence team who have gone through the whole records and are fully prepared to make first-class submissions; similarly, the Defence, equally prepared to respond in a most capable manner to all the points raised by the Defence, because you would have studied in its entirety the whole records of the case; and a Trial Chamber who has to start from scratch. It will not be the case. We have been following the case just like you have and when you come to that moment, we will be as informed as possible, as informed as possible. So we should also be in a position to interrupt you at certain moments and ask questions and ask you to clarify this or clarify that if it is the case. Don't expect the Trial Chamber to come here on that day really ready only to hear what you have to say and then start doing its homework afterwards. So it will not be the case. We will continue doing our homework afterwards, and the homework will then of course focus on the submissions which wouldn't be able to focus upon not having heard them until you start with your submissions, but that will be the position. Now, time. What you said, Mr. Wubben, alarmed me a little bit because -- I hope I have misread you, because the way I understood you was that although until, say, a couple of days ago, basing yourself on the last -- most recent updated witness -- confidential witness list, we have a more or less clear indication when we are going to finish with the case of the Prosecution. And in spite of the fact that earlier on in the day, after hearing both you and Mr. Di Fazio, I got the impression that we might finish even earlier. I now sort of get the impression - I hope I have misunderstood you - that you yourself are having second doubts, second thoughts as to when you are going to finish your case. And if that is the case, I'm going to call upon you to explain and tell me when you intend to finish the case. If not today, you need to tell me this tomorrow or Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We expect to end the case by the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So then the problem more or less becomes more of a cosmetic one. Let me put it like this: It seems to me that as soon as you finish -- it makes a difference if you finish -- if you rest your case on a Friday and we start on a Monday, that's basically -- what's in between is a weekday -- is a weekend, two days, Saturday and Sunday. If you finish your case on a Monday, then you have the rest of the week plus the weekend. So I think what we need to discuss is this, because I do not equiparate, but on the same standard weekdays when you are also expected -- I know that we all work on weekdays, all of us, not just you. And I also know how sometimes the pressure of work requires that you, in particular, work very hard on weekdays -- on weekends. I think that need not be the case for the purpose of Rule 98. I think that saying if the Prosecution case is rested on a Friday, that we should start immediately on a Monday. I think that can reasonably be avoided. That can reasonably avoided, provided this does not mean that it would entail much delay. So what I would suggest is the following: End of the May -- of the month would be what day? Tuesday. So if -- let's assume -- and the understanding is that there will be flexibility as we approach the date. We may change, obviously. What we are saying is just by way of giving an indication what to expect. Let's imagine for the time being that Mr. Wubben -- that the Prosecution, sorry, rests its case either on Monday, the 30th, or Tuesday, the 31st of May -- of May, May, May, May. Of May. That's a Monday or a Tuesday. Mr. Jones, since you would be the first one to go -- when I say "Mr. Jones," I mean the Defence. It's -- but I would take it since you are more familiar with this procedure that you will be dealing with this. You said you would roughly need two days to -- for your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Assuming that we finish the Prosecution case on a Monday or on a Tuesday, when would you prefer to start, the following Monday or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, our proposal was really to go right ahead. So it would be disingenuous of me to give myself an extra three or four days to prepare. Having said that, if we finish the trial in mid-week, starting the next Monday means that we would have a week, depending on how long Your Honour decides the Prosecution should have. But starting with a fresh week would make sense, that so would be the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I thought, too. So basically that would mean that you would start on the -- Monday, the 6th of June. It's not a holiday, is it? Please watch out if we have any holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a holiday in Ireland according to my diary, but none of us are Irish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have Italian and French blood, but not Irish, although I drink Guinness, of course. We all do, probably. That would mean, basically -- my idea is the following -- we don't have. If Mr. Jones takes Monday and Tuesday, that is, the 6th and the 7th of June, provided that there is no real, serious reason for a longer interval of time, I would suggest that you start the Monday after, which would be the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 13th, yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would prefer to have a longer interval in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Why, because, Your Honour, as we don't know what the position of the Defence will be and working on it, they are already in a position to work on it and we have to prepare to address it fully. So we would advise the Court to take into consideration that we prefer more time than a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will come back to you after we have discussed this because this is the agreement that we have. We will hear what you have to say and then we will obviously talk this, discuss among ourselves and come back to you on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, two things really. If the Prosecution has a delay after our motion and their response, then the Defence equally will have to request an -- a similar delay before we make our reply. What's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just wonder whether the Prosecution has a misconception about Rule 98 bis. We will be saying that they have not produced sufficient evidence for the counts, and so they can prepare as of this very moment to argue that there is sufficient evidence for each of the counts and each of the elements. That's 90 per cent of the work done. It really -- in my submission it would be a mistake to draw it out, given that there are other events this June which means that the procedure would get protracted into July. And in your submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, really, definitely. Forget -- for -- I simply don't even want to hear the word "July." It's -- forget it. It's -- otherwise I can't even face my other colleagues on this issue. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That is not our intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's because we have a right to reply, that's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the thing is this. Because you are adult enough and mature enough to understand how I have been moving. I could have -- taking advantage of what Mr. Jones himself had stated, I could have said, Prosecution will finish Monday or Tuesday of -- 30th or 31st of May. Mr. Jones, I give you Wednesday and Thursday to prepare, or I give you Wednesday, if you agree, and you make your submissions Thursday and Friday, they would have had one day. And then I could easily look at you and say, And you, Mr. Wubben, will have the weekend, maybe Monday because I will expect you to rest during the weekend and you will make your final submissions Tuesday and Wednesday. And we would have finished in seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're amenable to that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know you are. And that's why instead of suggesting that, I said let's take the three days -- remaining days of the week plus the weekend, which would make it five, because it would justify me looking towards you and saying you will have exactly the same, another five days. Because otherwise the message that I get from the Defence is that with one day or even less they would be prepared. In fact, Mr. Jones has practically for all intents and purposes repeated the same words that I said to my colleagues earlier on in the week when we were discussing these matters. I said that knowing that Mr. Jones will probably handling this and knowing which jurisdiction he comes from, the expectation is that he will stand up and he will go through the counts in the typical way in which we are used to without involving in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just say, Your Honour, the reason is that -- lest it be thought that I'm proposing to prepare in one day, the fact is that we're preparing it the whole time. We have CaseMap, and I think so does the Prosecution have CaseMap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And so should be the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're all in a position to prepare this as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, will you please bear me a moment to have an internal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, of course. If you want us to leave the courtroom, we will do so as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it will be short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see a smile on your face, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I on yours. That's shared, Your Honour. Your Honour, with a view to starting indeed after a week, we can agree upon that. We advise to the Trial Chamber that we might put in, as you stated yourself, that we should be flexible and not fixed on the date. We might put in a caveat, indeed, that whenever there is a slight issue that needs some more time for preparing, that we can get back to the Court and do a submission in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So for the time being the idea is the following, that basing myself -- or ourselves on what Mr. Wubben said, Prosecution is expected to conclude its case by not later than the 31 -- Tuesday, the 31st of May. The Defence will then have two days within which to make oral submissions under -- under Rule 98 bis, starting from Monday, the 6th of June. The Prosecution will make their submissions on -- also on -- under Rule 98 bis on the 13th of June, and likewise they will have two days maximum for making those submissions. There will then be a break of one day, which would enable the Defence to respond, to reply. And any final submissions will be concluded on that day. That would be, therefore, the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th of June. 16th of June. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With a view to the right to reply, do we have a right to reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. Usually not, but -- I mean, our duty for the time being under the Rule is to hear submissions from the parties. So I would interpret that to mean that since we have decided -- there's nothing written, but it stands to logic that the Defence goes first and you respond and they have a right to reply. If there is anything left which is worth mentioning, I don't see why we should put a closure on you, Mr. Wubben. Please, do try to understand that this is not a competition between the Trial Chamber and the parties; it's a trial in which we try to cooperate with you to ensure that justice is done and is also seen to be done. So that's our approach. Then, this is something that we have tried to -- we have discussed among ourselves. We will have business to transact the third week of June, as you know. As soon as we have had business -- have transacted their business, it is our intention to hand down the oral decision without delay, practically immediately after. However, if as a result of the business that we would be transacting during the third week we feel the need to come back to you on any issue, then we will come back to you on any issue on that or those issues which might need some clarification if it's the case. So the position is as follows. We thought it fit -- we would have probably -- not probably, certainly have been in a position to decide the matter before we transacted that business on the third of -- week of June, but it is our agreement that we would be -- we would feel much more comfortable with ourselves and with our conscience, basically, if we handed down our decision during -- after already the end of that week. Right. I think I have made myself understood. If you have any further questions in that regard, please let us know. We think that -- we believe that it is fit and proper that if that business is to be transacted, then obviously it should precede the Rule 98 bis decision. And then we will see what the situation will be at the end of the day. I think I have dealt with -- let me just check on my notebook whether -- I don't think I have left anything. If there are any further issues that you would like to raise in this context, please do, please do so. I think we have covered the whole terrain and more or less I think there is agreement on the basic points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just have one moment to inquiry with my colleague on one matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was just to mention one issue. In the unlikely event, as we say, that there will be a Defence case, we would need at some point to think about scheduling, obviously, for that so that we can plan our witnesses. There will be -- there would be a pre-Defence conference, et cetera, so it's really just to mention that at some stage we would have to schedule -- schedule either a pre-Defence hearing or at least give us some indication of when the Defence case, if it happens, would start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you for raising that issue, Mr. Jones. Of course we don't know if and to what extent the case may continue -- will continue. That's a pleasure as yet to come. But if it continues, then obviously there is -- your concern is our concern. So you can rest assured that we will not, as happens in domestic jurisdictions, the moment the Prosecution finishes its -- my first trial as a very young lawyer, age 21, I was asked by the judge then to come forward and assist a client who had just been abandoned by his lawyer and the judge wouldn't listen. He wanted the trial to start -- continue. He gave me one hour and a half to study the case and then the trial started. This was my first trial by jury. And as soon as the Prosecution case was concluded, it was not even five minutes' break, you stand up. This is how it is in our jurisdictions. But it will not be like that here. You will have what we will consider to be ample time, not necessarily will coincide with what you consider to be sufficient time, but we will of course deal with that as if and when we come to it, and you will have -- You mentioned pre-Defence conference. That is not mandatory according to the Rules, it's optional, but of course we would entertain such a request if it is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. First of all, I was going to say I trust that Your Honour had an acquittal for your first trial, but I won't inquire. But really it's for us to know whether we need to have witnesses ready in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had him acquitted on the charge which was of grievous bodily harm. He was finally found guilty of slight bodily harm. That's it, which wouldn't have warranted trial by jury in the first place. But let's bring this sitting to an end here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was just if we needed witnesses here in July. That's all we need to -- not to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we are fully aware that 23rd of July we go on recess in any case. So if we are talking -- if we are talking about the Rule 98 bis decision being given towards the end of June or at the latest the very early -- earliest in July, I don't think there is a point in worrying about this issue any further, at least for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have understood my language. All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And we will reconvene on Friday, now, I take it. Friday in the morning. Please correct me. I think this whole week is in the morning. In the morning, and we will start with the testimony of the witness that you mentioned. Yeah, but I will -- we can do it -- On that Friday we are going to try and do it this way like we did it last time because Judge Eser needs to leave the courtroom a little bit earlier. We will have one break instead of the usual two, and we will finish at around about half 1.00 or something like that or -- yeah, or something like that. Anyway, that's the idea. So that you schedule your examination-in-chief accordingly. Thanks. And we will not be sitting, of course, on the 13th as you all know. It's not because of this scaramanzia, Friday the 13th, but that we agreed that we need that day for deliberations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
